import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Expansion of $(1 - x)/(1 - 2 x + 3 x^2)$

This sequence is the expansion of $(1 - x)/(1 - 2 x + 3 x^2)$ in powers of $x$.
It satisfies the linear recurrence relation $a(n) = 2 a(n-1) - 3 a(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$,
with initial values $a(0)=1$ and $a(1)=1$.

*References:*
- [A087455](https://oeis.org/A087455)-/

namespace OeisA87455

/-- The primary defining sequence `a`, satisfying $a(n) = 2 a(n-1) - 3 a(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$,
with initial values $a(0)=1$ and $a(1)=1$. -/
def a : ℕ → ℤ
  | 0 => 1
  | 1 => 1
  | n + 2 => 2 * a (n + 1) - 3 * a n

/-- The leading decimal digit of a natural number. -/
def leadingDigit (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  n / 10 ^ ((Nat.digits 10 n).length - 1)

/-- A sequence of integers satisfies Benford's law if for each digit $d \in \{1, \dots, 9\}$,
the asymptotic relative frequency of terms with leading decimal digit $d$ is $\log_{10}(1 + 
    1/d)$. -/
def SatisfiesBenford (s : ℕ → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∀ d ∈ Finset.Icc 1 9,
    Filter.Tendsto
      (fun N : ℕ =>
        ((Finset.range N).filter (fun n => leadingDigit (s n).natAbs = d)).card / (N : ℝ))
      Filter.atTop
      (nhds (Real.log (1 + 1 / (d : ℝ)) / Real.log 10))

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 0. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_0 : a 0 = 1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 1. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_1 : a 1 = 1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 2. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_2 : a 2 = -1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 3. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_3 : a 3 = -5 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 4. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_4 : a 4 = -7 := by rfl

/--
It is an open question whether or not this sequence satisfies Benford's law
[Berger-Hill, 2017; Arno Berger, email, Jan 06 2017]. - N. J. A. Sloane, Feb 08 2017-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 60]
theorem conjecture : answer(sorry) ↔ SatisfiesBenford a := by
  sorry

end OeisA87455

findings.description: Lines 45–51 define only the first-digit law: nine limiting frequencies for digits 1 through 9. The cited source defines Benford's law using the entire significand distribution, equivalently all finite leading-digit blocks. These predicates are not equivalent. For example, let c(n) be the leading digit of 2^n, viewed as an integer. This sequence has exactly the required first-digit frequencies, but its significands are integers 1,…,9. In particular, its significand equals 1 with density log₁₀(2), whereas the full Benford condition requires density 0 for significand ≤ 1. Consequently, `OeisA87455.conjecture` currently asks only the first-digit version of the cited question.
findings.source_evidence: OEIS A087455 asks whether this sequence satisfies Benford's law and cites Berger–Hill (2017). In “What is Benford's Law?”, Notices AMS 64(2), p. 133, the authors define a Benford sequence by requiring, for every 1 ≤ s < 10, that {n : S(x_n) ≤ s} have natural density log₁₀(s). Page 132 explicitly describes the first-digit law as a consequence. https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/notices/201702/rnoti-p132.pdf . The paragraph immediately following Definition 2.1 in Berger–Eshun, “A characterization of Benford's Law in discrete-time linear systems,” author preprint p. 4, explicitly gives the leading digits of 2^n as a counterexample to the converse: https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~aberger/papers/benford_discrete_jdde.pdf .
findings.suggested_fix:
Replace the predicate by the full significand condition. A checked implementation is:

noncomputable def significand (z : ℤ) : ℝ :=
  (z.natAbs : ℝ) / (10 : ℝ) ^ (Nat.log 10 z.natAbs)

def SatisfiesBenford (s : ℕ → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∀ t : ℝ, 1 ≤ t → t < 10 →
    Filter.Tendsto
      (fun N : ℕ =>
        ((Finset.range N).filter (fun n => significand (s n) ≤ t)).card / (N : ℝ))
      Filter.atTop
      (nhds (Real.log t / Real.log 10))

Keep the conjecture's `answer(sorry) ↔ SatisfiesBenford a` form. The existing predicate could instead be retained under an explicitly first-digit name for a separate variant.

reformulations.difference: Lean defines the sequence recursively rather than as the coefficients of the rational generating function in the OEIS title. OEIS also explicitly supplies this recurrence.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For A(x)=∑ a(n)x^n, the initial values give constant coefficient 1 and linear coefficient −1 in (1−2x+3x²)A(x). The recurrence makes every coefficient of degree at least 2 vanish. Thus (1−2x+3x²)A(x)=1−x. Conversely, coefficient comparison gives exactly these initial values and recurrence; the denominator has constant coefficient 1, so the formal power series is uniquely determined.

sources_consulted: OEIS A087455, read through https://r.jina.ai/https://oeis.org/A087455 and the official data mirror https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A087/A087455.seq .

Arno Berger and Theodore P. Hill, “What is Benford's Law?”, Notices AMS 64(2) (2017), pp. 132–134; read through https://r.jina.ai/https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/notices/201702/rnoti-p132.pdf .

Arno Berger and Gideon Eshun, “A characterization of Benford's Law in discrete-time linear systems,” author preprint dated August 15, 2014: introduction, Definition 2.1 and following counterexample, Theorem 3.16, and Example 3.18; read through https://r.jina.ai/https://www.math.ualberta.ca/~aberger/papers/benford_discrete_jdde.pdf .
review.notes: All nine declarations were checked. The recurrence and five initial-value tests agree with OEIS. Lean experiments confirmed correct handling of signs, decimal boundaries, and real-valued frequency division, and proved every a(n) is odd and therefore nonzero. In /workspace/review/benford-check.lean, sorry-free proofs establish that replacing any sequence by its leading digits preserves the current predicate and that every such compressed sequence fails the source-faithful significand predicate. The fact that powers of two satisfy Benford's law is supplied by the literature, not proved in the scratch file. OEIS still records the question as open, consistent with the category. No repository files were edited.

not_demonstrated.reason: The concrete counterexample—leading digits of 2^n—requires proving its asymptotic first-digit frequencies, using nontrivial equidistribution arguments. The existing compression lemmas preserve the predicate only conditionally on an input satisfying it; they do not establish a concrete separating input. Refuting the proposed replacement alone or using the admitted conjecture would not meet the requested standard.

submission.summary: No short, honest demonstration meeting the concrete-input requirement was found. No trivial_proof.lean was created.
submission.gave_up_reason: This finding concerns a weakening of a real-valued asymptotic definition. Establishing the reported counterexample requires substantive limit/equidistribution mathematics rather than a trivial computation or proof.

submission.summary: Added a decimal-significand helper and replaced the nine first-digit frequency conditions with the full significand distribution condition for every real cutoff 1 ≤ t < 10. Updated the predicate's docstring and left the recurrence, tests, conjecture form, and status unchanged. The required compile command succeeds with only the existing `declaration uses 'sorry'` warning.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!

This sequence is the expansion of $(1 - x)/(1 - 2 x + 3 x^2)$ in powers of $x$.
It satisfies the linear recurrence relation $a(n) = 2 a(n-1) - 3 a(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$,

- [A087455](https://oeis.org/A087455)-/

namespace OeisA87455

/-- The primary defining sequence `a`, satisfying $a(n) = 2 a(n-1) - 3 a(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$,
with initial values $a(0)=1$ and $a(1)=1$. -/
def a : ℕ → ℤ

  | 1 => 1
  | n + 2 => 2 * a (n + 1) - 3 * a n

/-- The leading decimal digit of a natural number. -/
def leadingDigit (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  n / 10 ^ ((Nat.digits 10 n).length - 1)

/-- The decimal significand of an integer, ignoring its sign and taking the value `0` at zero. -/
noncomputable def significand (z : ℤ) : ℝ :=
  (z.natAbs : ℝ) / (10 : ℝ) ^ (Nat.log 10 z.natAbs)

/-- A sequence of integers satisfies Benford's law if, for every real $1 \le t < 10$,
the asymptotic relative frequency of terms with decimal significand at most $t$ is
$\log_{10}(t)$. -/
def SatisfiesBenford (s : ℕ → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∀ t : ℝ, 1 ≤ t → t < 10 →
    Filter.Tendsto
      (fun N : ℕ =>
        ((Finset.range N).filter (fun n => significand (s n) ≤ t)).card / (N : ℝ))
      Filter.atTop
      (nhds (Real.log t / Real.log 10))

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 0. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_0 : a 0 = 1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 1. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_1 : a 1 = 1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 2. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_2 : a 2 = -1 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 3. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_3 : a 3 = -5 := by rfl

/-- Value of the sequence `a` at 4. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_4 : a 4 = -7 := by rfl

/--
It is an open question whether or not this sequence satisfies Benford's law
[Berger-Hill, 2017; Arno Berger, email, Jan 06 2017]. - N. J. A. Sloane, Feb 08 2017-/
@[category research open, AMS 11 60]
theorem conjecture : answer(sorry) ↔ SatisfiesBenford a := by
  sorry

end OeisA87455
